sources: Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan Museum of Zoology), Balaeniceps rex (shoebill): stands 110 to 140 cm tall; bill resembles a wooden shoe and ends in a sharp curved hook; inhabits freshwater swamps and dense marshes, endemic to east-central Africa; eats mainly fish such as lungfish, bichirs, catfish and tilapia, plus watersnakes, occasionally frogs, monitor lizards, turtles, young crocodiles; hunts by 'stand and wait' or wading slowly; the 'collapse': head and neck stretch forward into the water so the bird over-balances and collapses forwards and downwards; prey is usually decapitated before swallowing; usually silent but bill-clatters, most often when greeting at the nest; lays one to three, normally two eggs; adults pour mouthfuls of water over the nest to keep eggs cool; usually only one chick remains by the end of the breeding cycle; https://animaldiversity.org/accounts/Balaeniceps_rex/

beats.say: This bird hunts by falling face-first into the swamp. Then it bites the head off its catch.
The shoebill. Up to four and a half feet tall, with a beak shaped like a wooden shoe.
It lives in the swamps and marshes of east-central Africa.
It hunts by standing still in the water, and waiting.
When a fish swims close, it throws its head and neck forward so hard, it loses its balance,
and collapses, face-first, into the water.
At the tip of that giant beak is a sharp hook.
It mostly eats fish, like lungfish and catfish. And water snakes.
Sometimes it eats monitor lizards, turtles, and even baby crocodiles.
When it greets its mate at the nest, it claps its beak together, over and over.
It fills its beak with water, and pours it over its eggs to keep them cool.
It usually lays two eggs. But by the end, usually only one chick is left.
And before it swallows its catch, it usually bites the head off.
Then it goes right back to standing still, like nothing happened.
So, would you stand next to one?
A bird shaped like a shoe, that eats baby crocodiles, and falls on its face to do it.
